extracted.intended_audience: science writers and freelance journalists (NASW community)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical ethical standards and decision‑criteria for science journalists—especially freelancers—about conflicts of interest, mixing corporate/non‑journalistic work with journalism, disclosure, and boundary setting. Draws on panel discussion opinions and real scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary between journalism and non-journalism work
rubrics_metrics.description: “What makes a journalist in 2015? … how much non‑journalism work does it take to no longer be considered a journalist?” — i.e., assess how mixing straight journalism with other (corporate/commercial) writing affects your status and obligations as a journalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize there are gray areas; freelancers commonly mix work. Consider whether the amount/type of non‑journalistic work undermines journalistic independence. The panelists debated that it can be managed ethically but that economic pressures complicate the line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether you are compromised
rubrics_metrics.description: Key question: can you write about corruption, poor science, or something bad about a person who is part of a company who pays you money? If you can’t, you are compromised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before taking on work, ask whether the paying relationship would prevent honest critical reporting. If it would, avoid covering that subject or recuse yourself. This is a practical litmus test offered by panelists (Erik Vance’s framing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure to editors and readers
rubrics_metrics.description: “Disclosure and transparency are critical when any potential conflict of interest exists. This means that the writer discloses any conflicts to his or her editor, and that the writer and/or editor discloses these to the readers when appropriate.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full disclosure to the editor is a baseline; public disclosure to readers should be made when it bears on credibility or could be perceived as a conflict. Use transparent language and err on the side of disclosure when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reporting on topics where you do corporate work
rubrics_metrics.description: “Writers who do corporate work on a particular topic should stay away from that topic or field in their journalistic efforts when possible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When feasible, refrain from covering beats or topics tied to corporate clients or sponsored work. Acknowledge practical difficulties: building expertise in an area may tempt you back to it, so weigh expertise benefits against conflict risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set clear, sharp lines you won’t cross
rubrics_metrics.description: “Spotting your own conflicts of interest is difficult since ‘we’re embedded. This is why sharp lines that you don’t cross are useful,’” — i.e., establish explicit personal/professional boundaries to simplify ethical choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create explicit rules (types of client work you won’t accept, beats you won’t cover, disclosure thresholds). Use these bright‑line policies to avoid self‑deception and make decisions defensible to editors and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for economic pressures but do not let them justify compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists noted the steep descent of compensation for freelancers and the necessity of taking on less‑journalistic work to make ends meet; this reality affects ethical choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that financial necessity can push journalists into ethically gray arrangements. Acknowledge the pressure openly and consider alternative strategies (different revenue streams, stronger disclosure, editorial recusals) rather than silently compromising standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use community/editorial judgment on real scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: The session ran real scenarios (details changed) and used attendee voting to gauge whether conflicts existed and what a writer should do, implying reliance on peer/editorial norms to resolve borderline cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When uncertain, bring scenarios to editors, peers, or professional forums (e.g., NASW) for collective judgment; community consensus and editorial oversight can help determine appropriate action (recusal, disclosure, or acceptance).
